passage: After football in a London park, Kwame and Diego sat on the bench with orange slices. "D-d-d-do you know what my g-g-g-grandad did?" Diego started. A bigger boy walking past said, "Just take a breath, mate." Kwame didn't look away from Diego. He kept chewing and waited, like it was the most normal thing in the world. "H-he fell in the p-p-pond. With his sh-sh-shoes on!" Kwame laughed so hard orange juice ran down his chin. "Was he okay?" "He was s-s-soggy!" Diego grinned. Kwame threw his peel in the bin. "Tell me the rest tomorrow."

qa.q: Where did Diego's grandad fall?
qa.a: In the pond, with his shoes on.

qa.q: What does Diego's grin at the end suggest about how Diego felt?
qa.a: It suggests Diego felt happy and respected, because Kwame listened to the whole story and enjoyed it.

qa.q: What did Kwame do that a wise listener would do?
qa.a: He kept his eyes on Diego, waited without finishing Diego's words, and responded to the story itself.

qa.q: How might Diego have felt about the bigger boy's comment?
qa.a: Diego may have felt hurried or singled out, since being told to take a breath treats the way Diego talks as a problem.

grounding: A peer meets Diego's stuttering by waiting, not completing sentences and not saying to take a breath, treating Diego as a full conversation partner.

passage: At the community centre library, five-year-old Jomon came up to the desk holding his father's hand. "C-c-c-can I have the b-b-b-book with the..." His lips pressed together and nothing came for a moment. Simran, the librarian, stayed kneeling at his height. She didn't guess. She didn't say "take your time." She just kept looking at him kindly and waited. "...the r-r-red tractor." "The red tractor book! We have two. One with flaps, one without. Which do you want?" "F-flaps!" "Flaps it is." She stamped his card and handed it to him, not to his father. Jomon hugged the book to his chest.

qa.q: Which book did Jomon want?
qa.a: The red tractor book, the one with flaps.

qa.q: What does Jomon hugging the book suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt proud and happy that he asked for it himself and got what he wanted.

qa.q: Which of Simran's choices showed respect for Jomon's pace?
qa.a: She waited without guessing or saying take your time, then gave him a real choice and handed the book to him directly.

qa.q: What would change for Jomon if Simran had guessed the book for him?
qa.a: He might feel his words didn't matter, and his father might end up speaking for him.

grounding: An adult meets a child's stuttering by waiting without completing sentences or giving advice, treating him as a full conversation partner.

passage: I'm Gurleen, from the flat next door. Tejas, five, rang my bell with a broken kite. "G-G-G-Gurleen, the k-k-kite, it, it..." His face went tight. I waited, looking at him. I didn't say "slow down"; my own uncle stutters, and says that makes it worse. "It fell off the r-roof and the string broke." "Oh no. Shall we fix it?" We sat on my steps with tape. Later his uncle said, "Tejas, take a breath first," and Tejas went quiet. I can't know what he felt, but later he told me all about the pigeon the kite nearly hit.

qa.q: What was wrong with Tejas's kite?
qa.a: It fell off the roof and the string broke.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling while waiting for Tejas to finish?
qa.a: Gurleen felt patient and caring, keen not to rush him, knowing from a relative how "slow down" can hurt.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that respected Tejas's pace?
qa.a: Gurleen waited, kept looking at him, did not finish his words or tell him to slow down, and answered what he actually said.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when his uncle said "take a breath first"?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed or corrected, since he went quiet and stopped talking.

grounding: Shows an adult neighbour who waits, does not complete a stuttering child's sentences or tell him to slow down, and treats him as a full conversation partner.

passage:
Monday: During the animal game, Francis, five, said, "M-m-m-my one is a f-f-f..." Shreya shouted, "Frog!" Francis frowned. "No. Fox." He didn't talk for the rest of the game.
Wednesday: Their teacher read a story about a boy whose words came slowly, and the class talked about waiting for friends. Shreya listened with her chin on her knees.
Friday: At the sand tray Francis began, "My n-n-n-nani has a, a, a g-g-goat." Shreya waited, watching him, her mouth shut tight. "It ate her slipper!" Shreya squealed. "Tell me more!" Francis told her all about the goat until the bell.

qa.q: What animal did Francis actually mean on Monday?
qa.a: He meant a fox.

qa.q: How did Shreya seem to feel on Friday while waiting for Francis?
qa.a: She seemed patient and interested, working hard to keep quiet, then delighted by the goat story.

qa.q: What helped Shreya change how she listened?
qa.a: Hearing the story about waiting for friends to finish helped her learn not to guess Francis's words.

qa.q: How was Francis affected on Monday compared with Friday?
qa.a: On Monday he felt frustrated and stopped talking; on Friday he felt heard and told the whole goat story.

grounding: Shows a young peer learning to wait and not complete a stuttering friend's sentences, and treating him as a full conversation partner.

passage: The school van was already honking downstairs when Hafsa, five, grabbed her aunt's hand. "Kashish Khala, I d-d-d-dreamt a, a, a b-b-b..." Kashish wanted to rush; the driver was waving from the window. She bent down anyway and kept her eyes on Hafsa's. She didn't guess the word. She didn't say "take a breath." "...b-b-blue whale in our b-bathtub!" Kashish's mouth fell open. "A whale in the bathtub! How did it fit?" "It, it, it was a baby one," Hafsa said, very serious. Kashish laughed. "Tell me the rest after school, okay?" Hafsa nodded hard and ran for the van.

qa.q: What did Hafsa dream about?
qa.a: She dreamt about a blue whale in their bathtub.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt with the van honking?
qa.a: She probably felt rushed and pressured, wanting to hurry, but chose to stay patient.

qa.q: What did Kashish do that respected Hafsa's pace?
qa.a: She bent down, kept eye contact, did not guess words or say "take a breath," and responded to the story with real interest.

qa.q: How might Hafsa have felt running for the van?
qa.a: Hafsa likely felt happy and listened to, looking forward to finishing the story after school.

grounding: Shows an adult who, despite time pressure, waits, does not finish a stuttering child's words or tell her to breathe, and treats her as a full partner.

passage:
In the colony park in Nagpur, Vijay was trying to tell Sachin about his new kite. "It's a b-b-b..." His eyes squeezed.
"Say it fast!" called another boy from the swings.
Sachin didn't. He held the ball against his tummy and kept looking at Vijay, waiting.
"...b-big red one with a t-tail."
"A tail! How long?" Sachin asked.
Vijay stretched his arms wide and grinned. They talked about the kite until Sachin's Nani called him home.

qa.q: What colour is Vijay's new kite?
qa.a: It's a big red one with a tail.

qa.q: Why did Sachin keep holding the ball and looking at Vijay?
qa.a: He was curious and interested in the kite and patient enough to wait for Vijay to finish.

qa.q: Which choice worked better, Sachin's or the boy on the swings, and why?
qa.a: Sachin's, because waiting and asking a real question treated Vijay as a full conversation partner, while "Say it fast" added pressure.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel when Sachin asks how long the tail is?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and happy that Sachin cares about his kite, not about how he said it.

grounding: Sachin waits for Vijay's stuttered words without finishing them or rushing him, treating him as a full conversation partner.
